known_for: Deacon of Edessa who taught the church's faith in hymns and sermons, and who ran the city's famine relief.

key_works.title: The Nisibene Hymns
key_works.about: Songs from the years of the Persian sieges and the bishops of Nisibis.

key_works.title: Prose Refutations of Mani, Marcion and Bardaisan
key_works.about: Prose arguments against three rival teachers.

key_works.title: Homily Against Heretics
key_works.about: A metrical homily that names Bardaisan's hymns as poison with sweetness.

legacy_traces: Sozomen names his best-known pupils, Abbas, Zenobius, Abraham, Maras and Simeon. He reports it was said that Ephrem wrote three hundred thousand verses, and says his works were put into Greek in his own lifetime.
Sozomen adds that Basil, later bishop of Caesarea, greatly admired him. Jerome read in Greek a volume of his On the Holy Spirit and found the incisive power of lofty genius even in translation.
Gregory of Nyssa gave a speech in his praise, the account of his life nearest to his own time.
legacy_remembered: Honored in the Syriac church with the title malpono, teacher. His hymns shaped its ritual, and lessons from his sermons were appointed to be read in its regular worship.
Honored beyond Syria. Sozomen calls him the greatest ornament of the Catholic Church.
uncertain: The later Lives of Ephrem add wonders that the early writers do not tell. They say his father was priest of an idol in Nisibis, and that Ephrem's prayer sent a cloud of gnats against the Persian army. Those stories rest on writers long after him.
Palladius says he died in his cell a month after the relief ended, while Sozomen says after a few days. Most writers date his death to 373, and some to 378.

Sozomen tells that when men came to carry him off to be a bishop, he ran into the market-place, dragged his clothes and ate in public, until they took him for mad and left. He stayed a deacon all his life.
Sozomen and Theodoret blame Harmonius, Bardaisan's son, for the sweet tunes. In his own homily Ephrem blames Bardaisan alone.
